name: Programming, Data Structures & Algorithms
desc: C programming, algorithm analysis, stacks, queues, arrays, linked lists, sorting, searching, BST, AVL, graphs, Dijkstra

topics.name: Programming in C: Pointers, Arrays & Strings
notes: An **array name is a constant pointer** to its first element — `arr++`, `++arr` and `arr = other` are **compile errors**. `arr + 1` is legal (just an expression).
For `int s[5]` at 1000 (4-byte int): `s + 1` = 1004 (next int), `&s + 1` = 1000 + 20 = **1020** (next whole array).
`*((int*)(&arr + 1) - 1)` gives the **last element** of arr.
Partial initialisation fills the rest with zero: `int s[5] = {1};` → 1 0 0 0 0. Only the **first** dimension can be omitted: `int a[][2]` is fine, `int a[2][]` is invalid.
`const int *p` / `int const *p` = pointer to a **constant int** → `*p = …` or `++(*p)` is a compile error. `int *const p` = constant pointer (p itself can't change).
`int (*p)[5]` = pointer to an array of 5 ints. `int *p[5]` = array of 5 pointers to int.
Storage: **globals & statics → static/data area**, locals → **stack**, `malloc` memory → **heap**. A static local must be initialised with a **constant** (`static int x = num;` → compile error in C).

Strings: `strlen` stops at the first `'\0'` ("function\0" → 8; "VIT\0Chennai" prints "VIT"). Arrays can't be assigned (`str2 = str1` → error; use `strcpy`). `strcat(d, s)` appends s to d and returns d.
Structures hold members of **different types**; keyword is `struct` (not `structure`), and the definition ends with `;` → `struct a_struct {int a;};`.
C passes arguments **by value** — `malloc` into a parameter pointer does not change the caller's pointer.

topics.name: Algorithm Analysis & Recursion
notes: Growth order (slow → fast): **1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ**.
**Big-O** = upper bound, **Ω** = lower bound, **Θ** = tight bound. n² + 3n + 4 = O(n³) (true) but not Θ(n³).
If T1 = O(F) and T2 = O(F) then **T1 + T2 = O(F)** (sum rule). Product gives O(F²), not O(F).

**Master theorem**: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), a ≥ 1, b > 1, f(n) asymptotically **positive**. Compare f(n) with n^(log_b a): smaller → Θ(n^log_b a); equal (×logᵏn) → Θ(n^log_b a · log^(k+1) n); bigger (+ regularity) → Θ(f(n)).
Master theorem **cannot** be used when f(n) is negative (e.g. −n² log n), a < 1, or the gap is not polynomial (e.g. n/log n with n^log_b a = n).
Common recurrences: T(n)=T(n/2)+1 → log n (binary search); T(n)=2T(n/2)+n → n log n (merge sort); T(n)=T(n−1)+n → n²; T(n)=2T(n−1)+1 → 2ⁿ (Tower of Hanoi).
**Recursion** = less code, easier to write, but uses **more memory** (call stack). Iteration = usually faster/leaner.
**Tail recursion**: the recursive call is the last action. **Non-tail recursion**: there is a pending operation after the call. **Indirect recursion**: A calls B, B calls A.
Backtracking: a node is **promising** if it can still lead to a complete solution; non-promising nodes are pruned.

topics.name: Stack & its Applications
notes: **Stack = LIFO** (Last In First Out). Operations: push, pop, peek/top. Pop on empty → **underflow**; push on full → **overflow**.

Stack applications: **function calls/recursion**, **reversing**, **infix → postfix conversion**, **postfix evaluation**, parenthesis matching, undo, DFS, backtracking. NOT for sorting or printing in the original order.
**Infix → postfix uses a stack of operators**; postfix evaluation uses a stack of operands.
**Prefix evaluation**: scan right → left. **Postfix evaluation**: scan left → right; on an operator pop 2 (second popped is the left operand).
Valid pop sequences: once a number is popped, any **earlier-pushed** numbers still in the stack must come out in **reverse push order**.
Stack using queues: **2 queues** is the efficient standard way; the **minimum is 1 queue** (rotate after each push). Queue using stacks: **2 stacks**.
Number of valid stack permutations of n distinct items = **Catalan number** C(2n,n)/(n+1).

topics.name: Queue, Circular Queue & Deque
notes: **Queue = FIFO**. Insert at **rear** (enqueue), delete from **front** (dequeue).
**Circular queue** reuses space: `rear = (rear + 1) % SIZE` on insertion, `front = (front + 1) % SIZE` on deletion.

Circular queue (keeping one slot free) is **full when (rear + 1) % SIZE == front** (i.e. front = rear + 1, or front = 0 and rear = MAX − 1); **empty when front == rear** (or front = −1 in the count-based version).
**Deque** = insert/delete at both ends. **Input-restricted deque**: insert at one end only, delete at both. **Output-restricted deque**: delete at one end only, insert at both.
**Priority queue**: served by priority (usually a heap). Used in Dijkstra, Prim, scheduling.
Queues are used directly for **scheduling and resource allocation** (CPU/printer queues), BFS, buffering. Circular queues suit round-robin turns (e.g. players in a multiplayer game).
Deque using a **singly** linked list: deleting from the rear is **O(n)** (you must find the previous node). A doubly linked list makes it O(1).
Reversing a queue recursively: dequeue x, reverse the rest, enqueue x.

topics.name: Arrays: Storage & Address Calculation
notes: Number of elements in A(L : U) = **U − L + 1**. AAA(5:50) → 46; BBB(−5:10) → 16.
**Row-major** (C): Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + [(i − L₁)·N + (j − L₂)]·w, where N = number of columns.
**Column-major** (Fortran): Addr(A[i][j]) = Base + [(j − L₂)·M + (i − L₁)]·w, where M = number of rows.
Array access by index is **O(1)**; insertion/deletion in the middle is **O(n)** (shifting).
**Sparse array/matrix** stores only non-zero (non-null) entries — {1, null, null, null, null, 10} has normal size 6, sparse size 2.
Arrays give excellent **spatial locality** (contiguous memory), which caches exploit.
A **polynomial** is conveniently stored as a linked list of (coefficient, exponent) nodes.

topics.name: Linked Lists
notes: **Singly linked list**: node → next. Last node's next = NULL.
**Doubly linked list**: node has **prev and next** pointers — O(1) deletion when you have the node.
**Circular linked list**: last node points back to the **first** node — no NULL in any next field. Singly circular: next only. Doubly circular: head→prev = tail, tail→next = head.
Linked list access is **O(n)** (sequential), insertion/deletion at a known position is **O(1)**.
In a 2-node circular doubly list: head→next = tail, head→prev = tail, tail→next = head, tail→prev = head.
**Cursor implementation** simulates linked lists with an array; free cells are kept in a free list at CURSOR_SPACE[0]. Putting node p back at the front of that free list = **releasing (freeing)** it.
Detecting a cycle: **Floyd's tortoise and hare** (slow and fast pointers).

topics.name: Sorting Algorithms
notes: **Bubble sort**: swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; **number of swaps = number of inversions**. With an early-exit flag, best case O(n) (already sorted). Worst/avg O(n²). Stable.
**Insertion sort**: insert each element into the sorted left part. Best O(n), worst O(n²). Even with **binary search** to find the position, worst stays **O(n²)** (shifting).
**Selection sort**: always O(n²) comparisons, at most n−1 swaps; not stable.

**Quick sort**: partition around a pivot; avg O(n log n), **worst O(n²)** (bad pivot, e.g. already sorted with first/last pivot). After partition, the pivot is in its final place: all left smaller, all right larger.
**Merge sort**: always O(n log n), needs O(n) extra space, stable. **Heap sort**: O(n log n), in place, not stable.
**Counting/Radix sort**: non-comparison, O(n + k) / O(d(n + k)).
Insertion sort inner loop: `while (j > 0 && arr[j-1] > value) { arr[j] = arr[j-1]; j--; }`.

topics.name: Searching & Hashing
notes: **Linear search**: O(n), works on unsorted data. **Binary search**: O(log n), needs **sorted** data with random access.
Binary search mid = ⌊(low + high)/2⌋. If key > a[mid] → low = mid + 1, else high = mid − 1.
Max comparisons for binary search on n items ≈ **⌊log₂n⌋ + 1** (e.g. 1000 items → 10).
**Hashing**: average O(1) search. Collisions handled by **chaining** (linked lists) or **open addressing** (linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing).
**Load factor** α = n / table size. Linear probing suffers from **primary clustering**.
For a sorted array in descending order: max = first element O(1), min = last element O(1).

topics.name: Binary Trees & Binary Search Trees
notes: Height h (in edges): **max nodes = 2^(h+1) − 1**; max **internal** nodes = 2^h − 1; max leaves = 2^h. Level i has at most 2^i nodes.
**Full binary tree** (every node has 0 or 2 children): n = 2·(leaves) − 1 → always **odd**. A **perfect** tree has 2^k − 1 nodes (1, 3, 7, 15, 31 …).
In any binary tree: **leaves = (nodes with 2 children) + 1**.
A binary tree **can be empty** (zero nodes), so "it must have at least one node" is NOT valid.
Traversals: **Inorder** L-N-R (gives sorted order in a BST), **Preorder** N-L-R, **Postorder** L-R-N, **Level order** uses a queue.
**BST**: left < node < right. Search/insert/delete O(h): O(log n) balanced, **O(n) skewed**. Checking whether a tree is a BST: inorder traversal must be increasing → **O(n)**.
Number of distinct binary trees with n unlabelled nodes = Catalan number C(2n, n)/(n + 1) (n = 3 → 5).
Delete a node with 2 children in a BST → replace it with its **inorder successor** (min of the right subtree) or inorder predecessor.

topics.name: AVL Trees
notes: **AVL tree** = self-balancing BST where every node's **balance factor** = height(left) − height(right) ∈ {−1, 0, +1}.
Search, insert, delete in AVL = **O(log n)** in the worst case.
Rotations: **LL case → single right rotation**, **RR case → single left rotation**, **LR case → left-right double rotation**, **RL case → right-left double rotation**.
Minimum nodes in an AVL tree of height h: N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1, with N(0) = 1, N(1) = 2 → 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20…
Insertion needs at most **one (single or double) rotation** to rebalance; deletion may need O(log n) rotations.

topics.name: Graphs: Representation, BFS & DFS
notes: Complete graph Kₙ has **n(n−1)/2 edges**. Number of spanning trees of Kₙ = **n^(n−2)** (Cayley): K₄ → 16.
Connected simple graph: **v − 1 ≤ e ≤ v(v−1)/2**. A tree has exactly v − 1 edges.
**Euler's formula** for connected planar graphs: **v − e + r = 2** (6 vertices, 7 edges → 3 regions).
**Adjacency matrix**: O(V²) space, O(1) edge check. **Adjacency list**: O(V + E) space — better for sparse graphs.

**BFS** (queue): level by level — shortest path in unweighted graphs, P2P networks, web crawlers, social "friends of friends". **DFS** (stack/recursion): topological sort, strongly connected components, cycle detection, maze solving.
BFS/DFS time = **O(V + E)** with adjacency lists, O(V²) with a matrix.
Graph traversal is harder than tree traversal: graphs can have **cycles** (need a visited array), **no fixed root**, disconnected parts, and multiple paths.
A **spanning tree** includes every vertex, is a subgraph, and is **always acyclic** with V − 1 edges. A DAG always has at least one vertex with in-degree 0.

topics.name: Shortest Paths: Dijkstra's Algorithm
notes: **Dijkstra** finds single-source shortest paths in graphs with **non-negative edge weights**. Greedy: repeatedly pick the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance, then **relax** its edges.
**Relaxation**: if d[u] + w(u,v) < d[v] then d[v] = d[u] + w(u,v).
Complexity: **O(V²)** with an array/matrix; **O((V + E) log V)** with a binary-heap priority queue.
Dijkstra **fails with negative weights** → use **Bellman–Ford** (O(VE), also detects negative cycles). All-pairs → **Floyd–Warshall** O(V³).
For unweighted graphs, BFS already gives shortest paths. Dijkstra works on directed or undirected graphs.
**MST algorithms** (not shortest paths): **Prim** (grow from a vertex, priority queue), **Kruskal** (sort edges, union-find).
